newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada introduces anti Helms-Burton legislation.
newsitem.headline: Canada introduces anti Helms-Burton legislation.

text.p: Canada's government on Monday introduced a bill aimed at retaliating against a controversial U.S. law designed to curb foreign investment in Cuba.
The bill was introduced by the speaker of the House of Commons on behalf of International Trade Minister Art Eggleton and Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy.

The bill, whose details were revealed in June, is a bid to counter the Helms-Burton law that is aimed at discouraging foreign investment in Cuba by penalizing foreign companies that do business with the Communist-ruled Caribbean island.
"Helms-Burton is an unwarranted move to extend the arm of U.S. law into trade between other countries," Eggleton said in a news release.

Canada's counter-legislation would allow Canadians to countersue in Canadian courts to recover damages awarded by U.S. courts under Helms-Burton. It would also allow Canada to issue "blocking" orders declaring that judgements handed down under any objectionable foreign law would not be enforced or recognized in Canada.
The bill, which would amend the Foreign Extraterritorial Measures Act, is not expected to meet any major hurdles in the House of Commons, the Canadian parliament's lower chamber.
"The FEMA changes are a deterrent against U.S. companies seeking to penalize Canadian firms doing legitimate business with Cuba," Eggleton said.

Under one of Helms-Burton's provisions, U.S. citizens and companies are allowed to sue foreign firms using property confiscated after the 1959 communist revolution in Cuba. Senior executives and shareholders of such companies, as well as their families, can be denied entry into the United States.

In July President Clinton suspended the right to file lawsuits under Helms-Burton for six months but his move was not enough to prevent Canada, Mexico and the European Union from pressing ahead with their proposed retaliations.
In fact, on Sunday the European Commission widened its proposed counter-measures to cover the effects of another U.S. bill which seeks to stop dealings with Iran and Libya.
In addition to the bill introduced on Monday, Canada, together with Mexico, is also considering a challenge of Helms-Burton under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

"These amendments send a strong signal that we are not backing down, and that we are prepared to take strong measures to protect both Canadian interests and International law," Axworthy said in the same press release.

The bill was presented by the Speaker of the House of Commons for the so called "first reading." It has to pass three readings and a vote by the House of Commons before it goes to the Senate for approval. Once approved by the Senate, it will become law. --Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau (613) 235-6745
